tldr: The Justice Department tells a Manhattan federal judge that training AI models on copyrighted text is fair use, siding with OpenAI and Microsoft against The New York Times.
Xi Jinping closes a four-day Egypt visit by calling for a new Middle East security architecture and signing chip, data-center and Suez industrial-zone agreements.
The 10-year Treasury yield hits 4.818%, its highest since November 2023, as traders price a real chance the Fed raises rates this month instead of cutting.
KFF Health News finds the Trump-Kennedy voluntary industry deals went largely unenforced: prior authorization fell about 11%, and the promised public dashboards never appeared.
The Strait of Hormuz stays effectively closed at six transits a day against a normal 85, with Brent near $95 after renewed US-Iran strikes.
OpenAI says its unreleased Astra model is the first to cross its Critical cybersecurity threshold, able to find and exploit unknown flaws without step-by-step human guidance.
Sanford Health closes its North Memorial deal after agreeing to 10 years of Minnesota attorney general oversight and $600 million in Twin Cities investment.
Nicolas Maduro asks a US judge to throw out his drug-trafficking indictment on head-of-state immunity grounds, eight months after US forces seized him in Caracas.
A federal judge refuses to break up Google's ad tech business, ordering auction-rule changes instead of the AdX divestiture the Justice Department sought.
A federal judge blocks Trump's second birthright-citizenship order, calling it almost certainly unconstitutional and based on a distorted interpretation of the Supreme Court.

items.headline: Justice Department tells a federal court that training AI on copyrighted text is legal
items.body: The Justice Department filed a statement of interest Tuesday with US District Judge Sidney Stein in Manhattan, urging him to hold that training large language models on copyrighted text is fair use. The filing, in The New York Times's consolidated case against OpenAI and Microsoft, states that "The United States has a strong interest in this Court rejecting any argument that training LLMs on copyrighted texts violates copyright law," and casts the American AI industry's success as a national security interest. A statement of interest is not binding; Stein decides the fair-use question himself. The Times criticized the filing publicly.
items.plain: To build a chatbot, a company first feeds it enormous amounts of writing, including news articles it did not pay for, so the system learns patterns of language. The Times says that is copying, which is what copyright law forbids. OpenAI says it is fair use, a legal exception allowing limited reuse of protected work. What is new is that the federal government stepped into a private lawsuit on the companies' side, arguing America needs to win the AI race. The government's view decides nothing; the judge can set it aside.
items.why: If Stein accepts the argument, the largest potential cost in AI development, paying for training data, mostly disappears, and every pending publisher suit weakens at once.

items.headline: Xi ends his first Egypt visit in a decade by proposing a Middle East security order without outside powers
items.body: Xi Jinping closed a four-day state visit to Egypt on Thursday. In a joint statement Wednesday with President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi, he called on Middle Eastern countries to be "masters of their own destiny" and to explore a new regional "security architecture" free of external interference, and said China was ready to help safeguard shipping routes. The two governments signed agreements on counterterrorism, data centers, semiconductors, critical-metals supply chains, wider use of each other's currencies, and a third phase of the China-Egypt industrial zone on the Suez Canal, which hosts about 200 companies and roughly $4 billion in investment. China's trade surplus with Egypt hit $12 billion in the first seven months of 2026.
items.plain: Egypt controls the Suez Canal, the shortcut between Asia and Europe that a large share of world trade depends on, and China has spent years building factories in a special economic zone beside it. The striking part is the language. Xi publicly proposed that Middle Eastern countries build a security system without outside powers, which in a region where the United States has kept bases for decades is a pitch to replace American influence. He made it while a US war with Iran has shut the region's main oil route. Egypt takes US military aid and is hedging, not switching sides.
items.why: China is offering the region an alternative security patron at the moment American power there is producing closed shipping lanes rather than open ones.

items.headline: Bond yields hit a three-year high as traders price a Fed rate hike, not a cut
items.body: The 10-year US Treasury yield touched 4.818% on Wednesday, its highest since November 2023, as markets repriced the odds that the Federal Reserve raises rates at its Sept. 15-16 meeting. The federal funds rate has sat at 3.50%-3.75% for five straight meetings. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh told the Jackson Hole symposium on Aug. 28 that he "would be hard pressed to describe broad financial conditions as restrictive." Futures moved from roughly a 35% chance of a September hike before that speech to between 58% and 70% after it; trackers published this week disagree by a wide margin. Brent crude, up more than 40% year over year, is the main channel.
items.plain: The Fed sets a short-term interest rate that feeds into mortgages, car loans and business borrowing. It has held steady most of this year. Now the war has pushed oil to about $95 a barrel, which lifts the price of nearly anything that is shipped or made, and the Fed chair has signaled he may raise rates to hold inflation down. That is unusual: central banks normally cut when a shock hurts growth, and raising into an oil shock squeezes households from both sides. Note the disagreement. Estimates of a hike run from 58% to 70%, so the market is not actually sure.
items.why: A hike would confirm the Fed now treats war-driven oil inflation as its problem to solve, which charges the cost of the conflict to American borrowers rather than absorbing it.

items.headline: The administration's voluntary deals with insurers and food makers went largely unenforced
items.body: An investigation published this week by KFF Health News found that the voluntary agreements the Trump administration and Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. announced with health insurers and food manufacturers have gone largely unenforced. Insurers covering roughly 80% of Americans pledged last summer to scale back prior authorization by January 2026 and to publish dashboards tracking progress. As of July, medical prior authorization had fallen about 11%, per the insurer trade group AHIP; no dashboards exist, and some signatories told KFF they will not implement all the promised changes. "These deals are often not transparent, so there's no way for the public to judge how meaningful they are," said Larry Levitt, KFF's executive vice president for health policy.
items.plain: Prior authorization is the step where your insurer decides whether it will pay for a scan, surgery or drug your doctor already ordered. It delays care and is one of the most disliked features of American insurance. Rather than write a rule, the administration got insurers to promise to do better on their own by January. The promise carried no penalty, and the reporting shows it produced roughly a tenth of the advertised change, with the public tracking tools never built. That is the mechanism worth noticing: a handshake announced at a press conference is not a regulation, and nothing happens when it is broken.
items.why: It is a test case for governing by voluntary pledge, and the result suggests the announcement, not the outcome, was the deliverable.

items.headline: The Strait of Hormuz is still shut in the sixth month of the war, and the oil price shows it
items.body: Six ships transited the Strait of Hormuz on Aug. 30 against a normal rate of about 85 a day, war-risk insurance for tankers is priced at multiples of pre-crisis levels, and Brent traded near $95 a barrel Thursday. Fighting reignited Aug. 30, when US Central Command struck two launchers on Larak Island that it said were preparing to seed the strait with sea mines. Iran's Revolutionary Guard answered with missiles and drones against the King Hussein and Al Azraq bases in Jordan and a drone over UAE waters; Jordan said it intercepted at least eight. The International Energy Agency has called the blockage the largest oil supply disruption in the market's history.
items.plain: The Strait of Hormuz is a narrow sea passage at the mouth of the Persian Gulf; before the war about a fifth of the world's oil moved through it. It is not blocked by a wall, it is blocked by risk. Insurers will not cover tankers that sail it and crews will not board them, so the ships simply stop, which works as well as a blockade. The oil still exists in the ground; it cannot reach buyers, and the pipelines that bypass the strait carry only a fraction. That gap is what is raising the price of fuel, and through fuel, of nearly everything else.
items.why: The Fed's rate debate, the bond selloff and Xi's pitch to the Gulf are all downstream of one waterway that has been closed for half a year with no reopening mechanism in sight.

items.headline: OpenAI says its next model is the first to cross its own Critical cyber threshold
items.body: OpenAI said in a blog post Tuesday that its forthcoming model, Astra, is the first to reach the Critical cybersecurity tier of its internal Preparedness Framework. By the company's definition, a model reaches that tier when it can identify previously unknown security flaws and build working exploits against many hardened real-world systems without a person guiding each step. OpenAI delayed the release, first reported by Axios on Aug. 7, while it built safeguards against cyber misuse and unauthorized model actions. Astra will ship broadly, but its most advanced offensive-security capabilities will be limited to vetted organizations in a coalition OpenAI calls Daybreak.
items.plain: Finding a security hole nobody knows about and writing code that uses it is skilled work that takes human experts weeks. OpenAI is claiming its next model does that end to end, on well-defended systems, on its own. The same skill is what defenders use to find and patch their own holes first, which is why the company is not withholding the model outright: it is giving the strongest version to a screened group and a limited version to everyone else. The catch is that this rests on OpenAI's own testing and its own definition of the threshold. No outside regulator verified either.
items.why: A company grading its own most dangerous capability and choosing who receives it is now the operative safety regime for offensive cyber tools, in the absence of a legal one.

items.headline: Minnesota let a hospital merger close by writing a decade of conditions into it
items.body: Sanford Health's acquisition of North Memorial Health closed Tuesday after the two systems signed a 10-year oversight agreement with Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison. Sanford, based in Sioux Falls, South Dakota, must invest $600 million in North Memorial over the decade, $500 million to expand Maple Grove Hospital and $100 million for Robbinsdale Hospital; keep Robbinsdale's Level 1 trauma center and other core services running for at least 10 years; honor existing collective bargaining agreements; and retain employees in good standing. Sanford abandoned two earlier attempts to merge with Minneapolis-based Fairview Health Services, in 2013 and 2022, after political and regulatory opposition.
items.plain: When two hospital systems combine, the usual worry is that the merged company closes unprofitable services and raises prices, because patients cannot easily drive somewhere else. Minnesota's attorney general did not block this deal; he priced it, extracting binding decade-long commitments in exchange for approval. That is a different tool from an antitrust suit: instead of arguing in court about future harm, the state wrote the harm out of the contract in advance. Whether it works depends entirely on enforcement, and this is the same buyer whose two previous attempts to enter the market collapsed.
items.why: State attorneys general are becoming the effective regulator of hospital consolidation, and conditional approval on these terms is a template other states can copy.

items.headline: Maduro asks a US judge to dismiss his indictment on head-of-state immunity grounds
items.body: Nicolas Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, asked a Manhattan federal judge this week to dismiss the drug-trafficking indictment against them, arguing that a head of state and a first lady are immune from US prosecution. That indictment was the legal basis for the US military raid on Caracas that captured Maduro on Jan. 3. He has pleaded not guilty; trial is set for June 1, 2027. Flores's lawyers wrote that the protection "is an attribute of Venezuela's sovereignty, and only Venezuela may surrender it." Judge Alvin K. Hellerstein set oral argument for Nov. 17.
items.plain: Sovereign immunity is the old rule that one country's courts do not put another country's leader on trial, on the theory that no government wants its own president hauled before a foreign judge. Maduro's argument is that the rule still shields him even though the United States removed him by force and no longer recognizes him as president. Only Venezuela's government could waive that protection, his lawyers say, and it has not. Nothing has been decided: this is a motion to dismiss, the judge hears argument in November, and the trial is set for June 2027.
items.why: How Hellerstein rules will set how far the United States can go in indicting a sitting foreign leader and then seizing him, a question with obvious application beyond Venezuela.

items.headline: Google keeps its ad tech business; the judge rewrites the auction instead
items.body: US District Judge Leonie Brinkema ruled Wednesday that Google will not have to sell its AdX ad exchange or its DFP publisher ad server, rejecting the structural remedies the Justice Department sought after she found in April 2025 that Google had illegally monopolized two advertising-technology markets. She adopted most of the behavioral remedies the two sides proposed, rewriting how Google's open-web display auction works: ending the "first look" and "last look" advantages Google's exchange held over rivals, and the unified pricing rules limiting how publishers set different price floors for different buyers.
items.plain: When a web page loads an ad, an automated auction picks it in a fraction of a second. Google owns the tool publishers use to sell the space, the exchange where bidding happens, and a large share of the buyers, and it had given its own exchange a first peek at bids and a chance to beat any rival's price at the end. The government wanted the company split up so it could not referee a game it plays in. The judge banned the specific advantages and left the ownership intact, so the fix now depends on Google following rules rather than on the conflict being gone.
items.why: A proven monopolization case ended in conduct rules rather than a breakup, which sets the practical ceiling for the remaining antitrust cases against large platforms.

items.headline: A judge blocks Trump's second birthright-citizenship order and says he misread the ruling he cited
items.body: US District Judge Deborah L. Boardman in Maryland on Wednesday preliminarily blocked the executive order Trump signed in August expanding the categories of noncitizen parents whose US-born children would be denied citizenship. It is the second time she has enjoined his effort to restrict birthright citizenship. Boardman wrote that the new order is "almost certainly unconstitutional" and that the administration relied on a "distorted interpretation" of the Supreme Court decision it cited as its authority. "The Supreme Court has spoken: Children in the certified class are 'citizens at birth,'" she wrote. "This Court must, once again, preliminarily enjoin enforcement of the President's most recent attempt to strip the right to citizenship from them." The injunction holds until the underlying class action is resolved.
items.plain: The 14th Amendment says people born in the United States are citizens, and courts have read that to include children of noncitizen parents for well over a century. Trump signed an order narrowing it, lost at the Supreme Court, then signed a second order in August citing that same Supreme Court ruling as permission for a narrower version. The judge who blocked the first order blocked this one too, and wrote that the administration had misread the decision it was leaning on. This is a preliminary injunction, not a final judgment, and it can be appealed; for now the order does not take effect.
items.why: Citing a Supreme Court opinion as your authority and having the district judge answer that the opinion says the opposite is the kind of loss that makes the appeal harder, not easier.
